title: tat tvam asi
tomorrow: a group project, one grade. whose work is whose, once it's done?

segments.voice: Yesterday in tat tvam asi, two views of the beginning, and Uddalaka's answer: Being alone, one without a second, wished to be many. Today he turns to something everyone does every night.

Midnight. One app, then another, then a third, and nothing lands. Then, mid-scroll, the phone slides out of your hand and you're gone. The Chandogya has a picture for nights like that. A bird tied to a post by a string. It flies off this way, then that way, finds nowhere else to land, and settles right where it's tied.
screen: `ONE APP, THEN ANOTHER.` → `A BIRD ON A STRING.` → `IT LANDS WHERE IT'S TIED.`

segments.voice: Learn from me about sleep, the father says. When a person sleeps, he has merged with Being. He has gone to his own. He hears it inside the word for sleeping, svapiti: sva, one's own, and apita, gone into. So in this teaching, falling asleep is a nightly homecoming. Then the bird. It flies in every direction, finds no resting place anywhere else, and settles where it's bound. The mind, he says, is the same. It flies everywhere, finds no rest, and settles in the breath, because the mind is bound to the breath. And at the end of this teaching, the father says it. That which is the finest essence, this whole world has that as its self. That is the real. That is the self. That you are, Shvetaketu. Notice where it lands. Not in a temple, not on a mountaintop. In a talk about sleep, said to one son, by name. And Shvetaketu doesn't say he's got it. He says: please, sir, teach me more. So be it, my dear, says his father.
screen: `SLEEP: GONE TO ONE'S OWN.` · `THE BIRD SETTLES WHERE IT'S TIED.` · `THE MIND IS BOUND TO THE BREATH.` · then, large: `THAT YOU ARE, SHVETAKETU.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle the way a bird lands: shoulders down, hands open in your lap, weight sinking into the seat. When the mind flies off, let it fly until it tires, then let it come down on the breath, the post it's tied to. Land as often as it takes.
Tat tvam asi: that you are. Here the father says it, right after the sleeper gone home and the bird that settles where it's tied.
Carry this: tat tvam asi, and the bird comes home to where it's tied. Rest well tonight.

fork.reveal: the father hears svapiti as sva, one's own, and apita, gone into. the sleeper has merged with Being: gone home, not gone missing.

original.note: Sanskrit: he sleeps. The father hears it as sva apita, gone into one's own.

trapdoor: what you thought: sleep is just switching off.

what a scholar hears: svapiti read as sva + apita at 6.8.1, the text's own word-play, then the refrain at 6.8.7 ending tat tvam asi, shvetaketo.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.1–2 (when a person sleeps he has merged with Being, gone to his own, so they say svapiti; as a bird tied by a string flies in every direction and, finding no rest elsewhere, settles where it is bound, so the mind settles in the breath, for the mind is bound to the breath)

Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (that which is the finest essence, this whole world has that as its self; that is the real; that is the self; that you are, Shvetaketu; please, sir, teach me more; so be it, my dear)

notes: Block 'tat tvam asi', day 3 of 9 (1752–1760). The myth says this is where the saying is first spoken (6.8.7); confirm.
The svapiti word-play (sva + apita) is the text's own explanation at 6.8.1, not a modern etymology; the lesson presents it as how the father hears the word. Confirm.
The lesson skips 6.3–6.7 (the three colors, food and mind, the fast) to reach the saying; a later day may want them.
'That is the real' renders satyam; some translators: 'the true'. Confirm.
